coma

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (UK) IPA(key): /ˈkəʊmə/
  • Audio (Southern England):(file)
  • (US) enPR: kōʹmə, IPA(key): /ˈkoʊmə/
  • Rhymes: -əʊmə
  • Hyphenation: co‧ma
  • Homophone: comber (non-rhotic)

Etymology 1

[edit]

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κῶμα (kôma, “deep sleep”).

Noun

[edit]

coma (plural comas)

  1. A state of unconsciousness from which one may not wake up, usually induced by some form of trauma.
    go into a coma
    slip into a coma
    come out of a coma
    • 1961, Harry E. Wedeck, Dictionary of Aphrodisiacs, New York: The Citadel Press, page 215:
      An a aphrodisiac, it results in santonin poisoning, followed by coma and death.
    • 2004, George Carlin, When Will Jesus Bring the Pork Chops?‎[2], New York: Hyperion Books, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 208:
      I wonder if a person who comes out of a coma feels refreshed and well rested.

Etymology 2

[edit]

    Learned borrowing from Latin coma (“hair of the head”), from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē, “hair”).

    Noun

    [edit]

    coma (plural comae)

    1. (astronomy) A cloud of dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet.
    2. (optics) A defect characterized by diffuse, pear-shaped images that in an ideal image would appear as points.
    3. (botany) A tuft or bunch, such as the assemblage of branches forming the head of a tree, a cluster of bracts when empty and terminating the inflorescence of a plant, or a tuft of long hairs on certain seeds.
    Translations

    • Czech: koma (cs) f
    • Dutch: coma (nl) f
    • Finnish: huntu (fi), koma (fi)
    • French: chevelure (fr) f, coma (fr) f
    • Galician: coma (gl) f
    • German: Koma (de) f
    • Greek: ουρά (el) f (ourá) (means also "tail"), κόμη (el) f (kómi) (means also "hair"), χαίτη (el) f (chaíti) (means also "mane")
    • Japanese: コマ (ja) (koma)
    • Polish: koma (pl) f
    • Russian: ко́ма (ru) f (kóma)
    Defect characterized by diffuse, pear-shaped images

    Latin

    [edit]

    Etymology

    [edit]

    Borrowed from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē, “hair of the head”). For sense 2, compare crīniō (“to cover with leaves, or hair”).

    Pronunciation

    [edit]
    • (Classical Latin) IPA(key): [ˈkɔ.ma]
    • (modern Italianate Ecclesiastical) IPA(key): [ˈkɔː.ma]

    Noun

    [edit]

    coma f (genitive comae); first declension

    1. The hair of the head.
      Synonyms: crīnis, capillus
    2. foliage, ears, blades, stalks of trees, grass (as though resembling hair)

    Scottish Gaelic

    [edit]

    Etymology

    [edit]

    From Old Irish cummae, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm-smiyo-, from *ḱóm (“beside, with, by”) + *sem- (“one, as one”).

    Pronunciation

    [edit]
    • IPA(key): /ˈkʰomə/

    Adjective

    [edit]

    coma

    1. indifferent, unconcerned
      Tha e coma. ― He couldn't care less.
      'S mi a tha coma dè thachras. ― I don't give a damn what happens.
      Coma de sin! ― Never mind that! Forget that!
      Is coma sin ― It doesn't matter.
    2. reckless, careless
    3. expressing dislike or even hate when used with le
      Is coma leam thu ― I hate you.
      Is coma leis an rìgh Eòghann agus is coma le Eòghann co-dhiù ― The king doesn't like Eòghann, but Eòghann doesn't care whether the king likes him or not.

    Derived terms

    [edit]
    • coma-co-dhiù

    Mutation

    [edit]
    Mutation of coma
    radical lenition
    coma choma

    Spanish

    [edit]

    Pronunciation

    [edit]
    • IPA(key): /ˈkoma/ [ˈko.ma]
    • Audio (Colombia):(file)
    • Rhymes: -oma
    • Syllabification: co‧ma

    Etymology 1

    [edit]

    Borrowed from Latin comma.

    Noun

    [edit]

    coma f (plural comas)

    1. comma (punctuation mark)
    2. (church) misericord
    3. (music) section
    Derived terms
    [edit]
    • coma decimal
    • coma flotante
    • comilla
    • con puntos y comas
    • en cero coma
    • punto y coma
    • sin faltar una coma

    Etymology 2

    [edit]

    Borrowed from Ancient Greek κῶμα (kôma, “deep sleep”).

    Noun

    [edit]

    coma m (plural comas)

    1. coma (deep sleep)
    Related terms
    [edit]
    • comatoso

    Etymology 3

    [edit]

    Borrowed from Latin coma.[1]

    Noun

    [edit]

    coma f (plural comas)

    1. (rare) mane
      Synonym: crin

    Etymology 4

    [edit]

    See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

    Verb

    [edit]

    coma

    1. inflection of comer:
      1. first/third-person singular present subjunctive
      2. third-person singular imperative
